# FDG7036

> DO specify the inner exception when wrapping exceptions.

Framework Design Guidelines, 3rd edition, section 7.2.3 Wrapping Exceptions.

## How it is checked

- Check: fdg (partial coverage)
- Diagnostics: FDG7036
- Automatic fix: no
- Severity: library warning, application warning, test warning
- Status: draft

Message: Pass the caught exception as the inner exception of '{0}'

FDG7036 reports a new exception created in a throw statement or throw expression inside a catch block, outside lambdas, anonymous methods and local functions, when the exception type has an accessible constructor with a System.Exception parameter and no argument of the creation is an exception. A parameterless catch, or a catch without a variable, is reported too, since it could declare one. An argument for an optional inner exception parameter that the creation leaves out does not count. Wrapping through a builder method (FDG7009) is not seen, so coverage is partial. There is no code fix.

## From the book

```csharp
throw new ConfigurationFileMissingException(...,e);
```

> **Jeffrey Richter:** It cannot be stressed enough how carefully this needs to be thought through. When in doubt, do not wrap an exception with another. An example in the CLR where wrapping is known to cause all kinds of trouble is with reflection. When you invoke a method using reflection, if that method throws an exception, the CLR catches it and throws a new `TargetInvocationException`. This is incredibly annoying because it hides the actual method and location in the method that had the problem. I have wasted much time trying to debug my code because of this exception wrapping.
